questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: What is the pattern of inheritance and genetic locus responsible for Wilson's disease?
opts: Autosomal recessive, caused by mutation in the ABCC2 gene on chromosome 10q
Autosomal recessive, caused by mutation in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13q
Autosomal dominant, caused by mutation in the HFE gene on chromosome 6p
X-linked recessive, caused by mutation in the ATP7A gene on the X chromosome
questions.exp: Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by dysfunction of ATP7B (Wilson ATPase) located on chromosome 13q. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: Match each inherited disorder of copper transport with its gene and clinical presentation — 1) Wilson's disease 2) Menkes kinky hair disease … A) ATP7A on X chromosome, causing severe copper deficiency, seizures, hypotonia, and brittle hair at 3 months B) ATP7B on chromosome 13q, causing copper overload presenting between 3 to 20 years
questions.exp: Wilson's is ATP7B on chr 13q presenting between 3–20 years; Menkes is ATP7A on the X chromosome causing copper deficiency with brittle hair and seizures at 3 months. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: What are the physiological quantities for daily ingestion of copper and its mucosal entry in the upper small bowel?
opts: Daily intake: 2–5 mg; Daily absorbed: approximately 1 mg
Daily intake: 10–15 mg; Daily absorbed: approximately 5 mg
Daily intake: 0.2–0.5 mg; Daily absorbed: approximately 0.1 mg
Daily intake: 20–30 mg; Daily absorbed: approximately 10 mg
questions.exp: Daily copper intake is 2–5 mg, of which approximately 1 mg is absorbed mainly in the duodenum via DMT1. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: Which of the following foods is NOT listed as a copper-rich substance on this page?
questions.exp: The three copper-rich substances listed are Chocolates, Nuts, and Mushrooms; citrus fruits are not listed. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: Fill up: Inside the duodenal mucosal cell, absorbed copper is sequestered by the intracellular protein ______.
questions.exp: The enterocyte diagram labels: 'metallothionase [metallothionein] : Sequestors Cu inside cell'. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: Why is Wilson's disease clinically impossible to diagnose in an infant under 3 years of age?
opts: Intracellular metallothionein requires a minimum of 3 years to become saturated and depleted of binding capacity
ATP7B expression does not activate until puberty
Maternal ceruloplasmin persists in neonatal circulation for up to 36 months
Intestinal DMT1 does not absorb dietary copper during early childhood
questions.exp: Metallothionein takes a minimum of 3 years to deplete its capacity, setting the minimum age of Wilson's presentation at 3–20 years. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: What is the fundamental molecular defect underlying ceruloplasmin abnormality in Wilson's disease?
opts: Total absence of apoceruloplasmin peptide synthesis by ribosomes
Excessive renal tubular excretion of intact ceruloplasmin
Failure to incorporate copper into apoceruloplasmin, leading to accelerated ceruloplasmin degradation
questions.exp: The defect is: 'Cu2+ not being incorporated in ceruloplasmin (fundamental defect) -> ↓ Ceruloplasmin degradation'. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: What baseline physiological concentration is expected for circulating ceruloplasmin, and below what level is it diagnostic of hepatic copper retention?
questions.exp: Normal serum ceruloplasmin is 20–35 mg/dL, whereas in Wilson's disease it is characteristically < 10 mg/dL. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: Assess the two statements on copper handling: I Excess systemic copper in healthy humans is cleared primarily via renal tubular filtration and enterohepatic recycling. II Apoceruloplasmin is a positive acute phase reactant and can appear falsely normal or elevated during systemic inflammation.
questions.exp: Statement I is false because biliary excretion is the sole physiological route ('Nil renal/enterohepatic circulation'). Statement II is true because apoceruloplasmin is a positive acute phase reactant. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with acute jaundice, marked fatigue, and pallor. Laboratory testing reveals low hemoglobin with negative direct Coombs test, low cholinesterase, mildly elevated AST and ALT, and a paradoxically low serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP). What metabolic liver disease must be urgently suspected?
opts: Wilson's disease presenting as acute fulminant hepatitis
Acute Hepatitis A infection with severe cholestasis
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with panacinar emphysema
questions.exp: Acute hepatitis in a patient <20 years with low Hb, low cholinesterase, mild transaminitis, and low ALP strongly indicates acute Wilson's disease. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's genetics, Menkes, copper transport and acute presentation
questions.q: Which of the following findings is NOT part of the classic constellation that raises suspicion for acute Wilson's disease in an adolescent?
opts: Low serum cholinesterase with mild transaminitis
Age < 20 years with unexplained fatty liver
questions.exp: Wilson's acute presentation features LOW alkaline phosphatase (due to zinc displacement by copper), not elevated ALP. (Book p1013)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Why does fulminant hepatic failure in Wilson's disease characteristically exhibit a depressed serum Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)?
opts: Circulating copper directly binds to and inactivates the canalicular MRP-2 transporter
Alkaline phosphatase is preferentially filtered and lost in urine
Massive copper release displaces zinc, an essential co-factor required for the active site of alkaline phosphatase
Copper toxicity causes selective transcriptional down-regulation of osteoblastic genes
questions.exp: The text explains low ALP as: '(Zn2+ & Cu2+ competing for ALP)' where excess copper displaces zinc. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: What is the typical presentation of chronic Wilson's disease before overt cirrhosis?
opts: Young asymptomatic patient with fatigue and mild transaminase elevation (<150 U/L) where ALT > AST
Severe right upper quadrant pain with transaminases >2000 U/L
Isolated massive ascites without any constitutional symptoms
Rapid onset of chorea within weeks of first symptom
questions.exp: Chronic presentation has no specific symptoms: 'Fatigue + enzymes (<150 U/L) ALT > AST ... Young asymptomatic pt. with rise in serum enzymes'. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Fill up: On abdominal ultrasound, cirrhotic Wilson's disease characteristically displays a mixed cirrhosis pattern with ______ nodules predominating over micronodules.
questions.exp: Ultrasound reveals 'mixed cirrhosis (macro > micro)'. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Which metabolic liver disease carries the 'maximum jaundice tendency' among all hepatic disorders?
questions.exp: The header explicitly highlights: 'Jaundice in Wilson's disease : maximum jaundice tendency'. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Match each type of jaundice observed in Wilson's disease with its specific etiology — 1) Pre-hepatic / Hemolytic 2) Hepatic 3) Post-hepatic / Obstructive … A) Acute and chronic hepatocellular necrosis (disease proper) B) Gallstones and cholestasis C) Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia in fulminant failure
questions.exp: Wilson's produces all 3 jaundice types: pre-hepatic via Coombs-negative hemolysis, hepatic via disease proper, and post-hepatic via gallstones/cholestasis. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: What ultrastructural mitochondrial abnormality on electron microscopy is characteristic of Wilson's disease?
opts: Concentric whorls of smooth endoplasmic reticulum (fingerprint bodies)
Giant paracrystalline inclusions inside the mitochondrial matrix
Disruption of the outer mitochondrial membrane with cytochrome c leakage
Tennis racquet appearance due to dilatation of the tips of mitochondrial cristae
questions.exp: Electron microscopy shows 'Tennis racquet appearance (mitochondria involved) d/t dilatation of tips of cristae.' (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Fill up: On liver histology, hepatocytes in Wilson's disease characteristically exhibit ______ nuclei due to glycogenic degeneration.
questions.exp: Histopathology lists: 'Glycogenated nucleus inside hepatocyte ... vacuolation of nuclei (glycogenic degradation)'. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Match each hepatotoxin or metabolic disorder with the specific hepatic lobular zone it affects — 1) Paracetamol and ischemia 2) Yellow phosphorus 3) Wilson's disease … A) Zone 2 (midzonal) B) Zone 3 (centrilobular) C) Zone 1 (periportal)
questions.exp: Zone involvement: Paracetamol is centrilobular (Zone 3), phosphorus is midzonal (Zone 2), and Wilson's disease affects periportal (Zone 1) hepatocytes. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Besides hepatocytes, in which hepatic sinusoidal cell type does excess copper deposit in Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: Histopathology notes: 'Cu2+ deposition inside Kuffer [Kupffer] cell.' (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: How many years typically elapse before neurological manifestations emerge in Wilson's disease (Neuro-Wilson's)?
questions.exp: Under Neuro-Wilson's, the text notes: '10 years for presentation.' (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, histology and cristae
questions.q: Assess the two statements on Wilson's disease: I Steatosis (fatty liver-like change) is a recognized histological feature of both Hepatitis C and Wilson's disease. II Neurological Wilson's primarily involves the head of the caudate nucleus while sparing the lenticular nucleus.
questions.exp: Statement I is true ('Steatosis: HCV & Wilson's disease'). Statement II is false because Neuro-Wilson's is hepatolenticular degeneration involving the lenticular nucleus. (Book p1014)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: What is the most common (m/c) clinical neurological manifestation in Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: Under classical neurological manifestations, item 4 lists 'Dysarthria (m/c)'. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Match each neurological feature of Wilson's disease with its clinical sign — 1) Facial grimacing posturing 2) Coarse arm tremor … A) Wing-beating tremors B) Risus sardonicus (dysphonic vacuous posturing)
questions.exp: Facial dystonia manifests as 'Dysphonic posturing (Risus sardonicus)', and tremor presents as 'Wing beating tremors'. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a rare neurological manifestation of Wilson's disease on this page?
questions.exp: Rare neurological features listed are ANS involvement, memory loss, and migraine; trigeminal neuralgia is not mentioned. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Fill up: In Wilson's disease, the Kayser-Fleischer (K-F) ring is caused by copper deposition in the ______ membrane of the cornea near the limbus.
questions.exp: The K-F ring is defined as 'Cu2+ deposits in descemet membrane near limbus especially in superior and inferior poles.' (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: What respective association rates are documented for corneal copper rings in patients presenting with liver versus brain disease?
questions.exp: K-F ring association is 60–65% in hepatic presentations and 95–99% in neurological presentations. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Besides Wilson's disease, in which of the following cholestatic conditions can a corneal Kayser-Fleischer ring occasionally be seen?
questions.exp: K-F rings can occur in prolonged cholestasis: Wilson's, PBC, PSC, and Familial cholestatic syndrome; not in acute hepatitis A. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: What characteristic lens abnormality is produced by copper deposition in Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: Item 2 under ophthalmic findings is 'Sunflower cataract'. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Match each organ system with its extrahepatic manifestation in Wilson's disease — 1) Endocrine 2) Renal 3) Blood … A) Proximal Renal Tubular Acidosis (Type-2 RTA) B) Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia C) Hypoparathyroidism
questions.exp: Other manifestations: Endocrine = Hypoparathyroid; Renal = Proximal RTA Type-2; Blood = Coombs negative hemolysis. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Which gastrointestinal organ complication is listed among the systemic manifestations of Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: Under other manifestations, the 'GI' branch lists 'Pancreatitis'. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: Assess the two statements on Wilson's disease: I Kayser-Fleischer rings characteristically disappear or regress following effective copper chelation therapy. II Wilson's disease produces distal Type-1 renal tubular acidosis with nephrocalcinosis.
questions.exp: Statement I is true ('Rx: Chelation therapy' leads to regression). Statement II is false because Wilson's produces Proximal RTA Type-2 (Fanconi syndrome). (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's neurological signs, K-F rings and multi-organ pathology
questions.q: A 19-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea, a history of two spontaneous abortions, dysarthria, and bilateral wing-beating tremor. Slit-lamp biomicroscopy reveals a golden-brown ring at the superior and inferior limbus. What is the definitive initial medical management?
questions.exp: The clinical picture demonstrates neurological Wilson's disease with K-F ring, managed with chelation therapy. (Book p1015)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: What serum ceruloplasmin screening thresholds rule out versus confirm Wilson's disease?
opts: > 50 mg/dL rules out Wilson's; < 30 mg/dL is confirmatory
> 10 mg/dL rules out Wilson's; < 2 mg/dL is confirmatory
> 35 mg/dL rules out Wilson's; < 15 mg/dL is confirmatory
> 20 mg/dL rules out Wilson's; < 10 mg/dL is confirmatory
questions.exp: Screening ceruloplasmin: > 20 mg/dL 'rule out wilsons', 10–20 mg/dL is intermediate, and < 10 mg/dL is 'Confirmatory'. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: In a patient with an intermediate ceruloplasmin level (10–20 mg/dL), what is the status of total serum copper versus non-ceruloplasmin-bound (free) copper?
opts: Total serum copper is elevated, while free copper is undetectable
Total serum copper and ceruloplasmin-bound copper are both elevated
Total serum copper is decreased, but non-ceruloplasmin-bound free copper is elevated
Total serum copper and free copper are both markedly increased
questions.exp: Total serum Cu is decreased because ceruloplasmin-bound Cu (90% normal) is markedly decreased (↓↓), whereas free copper is increased (↑), driving high urinary free copper. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: What is the critical diagnostic hepatic copper concentration on liver biopsy in Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: Quantitative copper estimation on liver biopsy has a 'Critical value : >250 µg/g dry wt.' (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Which two analytical techniques are specified for quantitative hepatic copper measurement?
opts: Neutron activation analysis or atomic absorption spectrometry
High-performance liquid chromatography or mass spectrometry
Western blotting or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
questions.exp: Quantitative hepatic copper is 'estimated by : Neutron activation Analysis or Atomic absorption spectrometry'. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Assess the two statements on serum ceruloplasmin: I Serum ceruloplasmin can be falsely elevated into the normal range during acute inflammation and high-estrogen states like pregnancy. II Non-ceruloplasmin bound copper (NCBC) is used to monitor compliance and efficacy following copper chelation therapy.
questions.exp: Both statements are true as noted in the box: acute inflammation/pregnancy cause false elevations, and NCBC monitors therapy. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Match each biochemical parameter in Wilson's disease with its diagnostic directional shift — 1) Serum ceruloplasmin and total serum copper 2) Basal 24-hour urine copper and liver biopsy copper … A) Increased (↑) B) Decreased (↓)
questions.exp: Biochemical parameters: Serum Ceruloplasmin ↓, Serum Copper ↓, Basal 24 hr urine Cu ↑, and Liver copper ↑. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Which triad of laboratory variables forms the Nazar prognostic index for Wilson's acute liver failure?
opts: Serum copper, ceruloplasmin, and urinary copper
ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and platelet count
Serum bilirubin, AST, and Prothrombin time (PT)
questions.exp: The Nazar prognostic index comprises S. bilirubin, AST, and PT. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: What is the drug of choice (DOC) for Wilson's disease, and what is its standard starting and maintenance dose range?
opts: D-Penicillamine; start at 250 mg/day and increase to 1.5 g/day
Trientine; start at 100 mg/day and increase to 500 mg/day
Zinc acetate; start at 10 mg TDS and increase to 50 mg TDS
Tetrathiomolybdate; start at 50 mg daily for life
questions.exp: D-Penicillamine is DOC; starting dose is 250 mg/day, increased to 1.5 g/day. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Why must oral D-Penicillamine always be taken on an empty stomach?
opts: It directly degrades dietary essential amino acids in the stomach
Food and dietary cations significantly chelate the drug and impair intestinal absorption
It requires gastric hydrochloric acid to convert into its active disulfide form
Food co-ingestion triggers severe immediate anaphylactoid reactions
questions.exp: The instructions explicitly specify: 'To be taken empty stomach' because food interferes with bioavailability. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Which of the following adverse effects is NOT listed under D-penicillamine therapy?
questions.exp: Adverse risks listed are Drug induced lupus erythematosus, membranous nephropathy, myasthenia crisis, Aplastic anemia, and Pyridoxine deficiency (give 25 mg); pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is not listed. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: What dose of pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) should be co-prescribed with D-penicillamine to prevent deficiency?
questions.exp: The book notes: 'Pyridoxine deficiency (Pyridoxine 25 mg to be given)'. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's screening algorithm, Nazar index and chelation pharmacotherapy
questions.q: Match each anti-copper agent with its specific clinical niche — 1) Trientine 2) Tetrathiomolybdate 3) Zinc … A) 50 mg TDS; induces metallothionein, competes with Cu for DMT-1, preferred in pregnancy B) Chelator for Neurological Wilson's disease (not widely available) C) 1–1.2 g/day; lesser side effects, not available in India, preferred in pregnancy
questions.exp: Trientine (1–1.2 g/day) has fewer side effects and is preferred in pregnancy; Tetrathiomolybdate is for Neuro-Wilson's; Zinc (50 mg TDS) induces metallothionein and competes for DMT-1. (Book p1016)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: Which classic midbrain sign on T2-weighted brain MRI is characteristic of neurological Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: The midbrain MRI photo and caption highlight the 'Face of giant panda' sign. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: Match each brain MRI finding in Wilson's disease with its neuroanatomical location — 1) Mercedes-Benz sign 2) Bright Claustrum sign … A) Hyperintensity in the thin gray matter claustrum lateral to the putamen B) Trisected hyperintensity in the pons
questions.exp: The Mercedes-Benz sign corresponds to 'Trisected pontine' hyperintensity; the Bright Claustrum sign shows bilateral claustrum hyperintensity. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: Which of the following MRI abnormalities is NOT illustrated on this page for Wilson's disease?
questions.exp: Illustrated MRI signs are Basal ganglia hyperintensity, Face of giant panda, Thalamic hyperintensity, Bisected pontine hyperintensity, Mercedes Benz sign (trisected pontine), and Bright Claustrum sign. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: What is the mode of inheritance and responsible gene in classic adult hereditary hemochromatosis?
opts: Autosomal recessive, defect in the hemojuvelin gene on chromosome 1q
Autosomal recessive, defect in the HFE gene on chromosome 6p
Autosomal dominant, defect in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13q
X-linked recessive, defect in the ferroportin gene
questions.exp: Hereditary hemochromatosis is autosomal recessive, caused by a defect in the HFE gene on chromosome 6p. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: At what stage of life does classic adult hereditary hemochromatosis typically become clinically manifest?
questions.exp: The book notes: 'Adult : 4th to 5th decade' for HFE-related hemochromatosis. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: Match each genotype of the C282Y HFE mutation with its clinical association — 1) Homozygous C282Y 2) Heterozygous C282Y … A) Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) and NASH B) Full-blown hereditary hemochromatosis
questions.exp: Homozygous C282Y causes hemochromatosis, whereas heterozygous C282Y is associated with PCT (Porphyria cutanea tarda) and NASH. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: Which non-HFE genes are responsible for early-onset Juvenile Hemochromatosis?
questions.exp: Non-HFE juvenile hemochromatosis involves 'Hemojuvelin transferrin receptor-2' and 'Hepcidin'. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Wilson's neuroimaging and Hemochromatosis genetics
questions.q: Assess the two statements: I Co-existing alcohol consumption markedly accelerates the progression to cirrhosis in patients with hereditary hemochromatosis. II The Bright Claustrum sign on MRI is pathognomonic for Wilson's disease.
questions.exp: Both statements are true: alcohol increases cirrhosis risk in hemochromatosis, and the Bright Claustrum sign is demonstrated in Wilson's disease. (Book p1017)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: Fill up: In the duodenum, mucosal iron absorption occurs across the apical enterocyte membrane via the transporter ______.
questions.exp: Fe2+ enters the duodenal cell across the apical membrane via DMT-1. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: Which transporter on the basolateral membrane of duodenal enterocytes exports iron into the systemic circulation?
questions.exp: Iron is exported across the basolateral membrane by Ferroportin (Fe2+ -> Fe3+). (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: What is the physiological role of hepatic hepcidin in iron homeostasis?
opts: It stimulates transferrin excretion into bile
It binds to and inhibits basolateral ferroportin, downregulating systemic iron absorption
It promotes apical DMT-1 synthesis in the duodenum
It directly converts ferrous iron (Fe2+) to ferric iron (Fe3+)
questions.exp: Hepcidin (produced by the liver) inhibits ferroportin (-), reducing iron absorption. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: How does mutation of the HFE gene cause iron overload in hereditary hemochromatosis?
opts: Direct over-activation of splenic macrophage phagocytosis
Complete failure of ferritin synthesis inside hepatocytes
Inhibition of urinary iron filtration by the glomerulus
Loss of HFE-mediated regulation leads to hepcidin deficiency and unchecked ferroportin iron export
questions.exp: HFE regulates hepcidin; HFE mutation leads to 'No regulation over Hepcidin -> excess iron absorption and abnormal deposition'. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: What is the single best screening test for Hereditary Hemochromatosis?
questions.exp: Transferrin saturation > 45% is explicitly designated as the 'Best screening test'. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: What is the normal percentage for transferrin saturation, and what formula defines it?
questions.exp: The formula is: (S. Fe / TIBC) x 100, which normally equals 33%. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: Match each biochemical iron marker in hemochromatosis with its directional change — 1) Serum Ferritin and Serum Iron 2) Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) … A) Decreased (↓), serving as an indirect marker of serum transferrin B) Elevated (↑)
questions.exp: In hemochromatosis, S. Ferritin and S. Iron are elevated (↑), whereas TIBC is decreased (↓) as an indirect marker of transferrin. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: Fill up: On liver biopsy, hemosiderosis in hereditary hemochromatosis characteristically demonstrates iron deposition predominantly in ______ hepatocytes, visualized with Prussian blue stain.
questions.exp: Histopathology shows: 'Iron deposition more in peripheral zone ... Iron deposition in periportal hepatocytes (Prussian blue stain)'. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: What histochemical special stain is used to confirm iron accumulation on liver biopsy?
questions.exp: The caption specifies: 'Iron deposition in periportal hepatocytes (Prussian blue stain)'. (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: A 48-year-old man with fatigue and elevated LFTs undergoes abdominal MRI. The scan demonstrates diffuse low signal intensity throughout the liver on T2 sequences, while the spleen shows completely normal signal intensity without iron deposition. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: In hereditary hemochromatosis, MRI shows: 'Iron deposition in liver (low intensity) & not seen in spleen' (sparing the spleen, unlike secondary hemosiderosis). (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening and liver MRI
questions.q: Assess the two statements on iron overload: I In hereditary hemochromatosis, iron accumulates heavily in both the liver and the spleen simultaneously. II Total iron binding capacity (TIBC) is an indirect surrogate marker of serum transferrin.
questions.exp: Statement I is false because MRI shows iron is 'not seen in spleen'. Statement II is true ('TIBC: ↓ (indirect marker of S. transferrin)'). (Book p1018)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: Match each organ involved in hereditary hemochromatosis with its characteristic clinical manifestation — 1) Pancreas 2) Heart 3) Skin … A) Slate grey hyperpigmentation and bronzing B) Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) in juveniles > restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCMP) C) Type 3c Diabetes Mellitus (bronze diabetes)
questions.exp: Pancreas involvement causes Type 3c DM; heart causes DCM (juvenile) > RCMP; skin causes slate grey hyperpigmentation and bronzing. (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: What type of crystal arthropathy and radiographic sign are seen in hemochromatosis arthropathy?
opts: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystal deposition with hook-like osteophytes
Monosodium urate needle crystals with punched-out periarticular erosions
Basic calcium phosphate deposition with rotator cuff calcification
Cholesterol crystal synovitis with bamboo spine fusion
questions.exp: Joint involvement features 'CPPD crystal deposition -> Pseudo osteoarthritis, Hook like osteophytes, Involvement of mcp/wrist joints'. (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: Which of the following joints is characteristically affected by pseudogout and hook-like osteophytes in hemochromatosis?
questions.exp: Hemochromatosis characteristically affects the 2nd/3rd MCP, wrist, and MTP joints; isolated 1st MTP podagra is classic for gout. (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: Why do patients with hemochromatosis develop hypogonadotropic hypogonadism?
opts: Massive circulating estrogen from portosystemic shunting
Pituitary iron deposition damages the pituitary stalk, suppressing GnRH, LH, and FSH
Direct iron toxicity to Leydig cells causing primary hypergonadotropic failure
questions.exp: Gonadal failure is 'Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (↓ GNRH -> ↓ FSH, ↓ LH)' caused by 'Pituitary deposition -> Acquired hypopituitarism : stalk involvement'. (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: Which triad of disorders is highlighted as causing acquired hypopituitarism with pituitary stalk involvement?
opts: Sheehan syndrome, Pituitary apoplexy, Lymphocytic hypophysitis
questions.exp: The three stalk involvement causes listed are Langerhans cell histiocytosis, Sarcoidosis, and Hemochromatosis. (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: What is the confirmatory investigation of choice (IOC) for hereditary hemochromatosis?
opts: HFE gene mutation analysis for the C282Y mutation
Percutaneous liver biopsy with iron dry weight quantification
questions.exp: The confirmatory test is explicitly labeled: 'Confirmatory test : HFE gene mutation analysis (IOC). For C282Y mutation.' (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: What is the first-line treatment of choice for hereditary hemochromatosis, and what is the target serum ferritin endpoint for transitioning to monthly maintenance?
opts: Weekly phlebotomy until serum ferritin drops below 50–500 ng/mL, then monthly
Continuous intravenous deferoxamine until serum ferritin is zero
Daily oral penicillamine until urinary iron excretion normalizes
questions.exp: Treatment: 'Weekly phlebotomy -> S. ferritin value < 50-500 ng/mL -> monthly once.' (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: For a patient with hereditary hemochromatosis who cannot tolerate phlebotomy due to severe congestive cardiac failure, what alternative therapy is indicated?
questions.exp: If intolerant to phlebotomy, the book specifies: 'S/C Desferrioxamine x 5 days a week'. (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: Which two organ complications in hereditary hemochromatosis produce IRREVERSIBLE damage that fails to improve despite aggressive iron depletion?
opts: Skin bronzing and pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction
questions.exp: The note emphasizes: 'Irreversible organ damage : Joint and gonads.' (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: Assess the two statements on hemochromatosis: I In patients with hemochromatosis and established cirrhosis who undergo successful liver transplantation, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is completely eliminated. II Weekly phlebotomy yields very good clinical response if initiated before cirrhosis develops.
questions.exp: Statement I is false because 'Post transplant risk of HCC present'. Statement II is true ('Response is good if cirrhosis absent'). (Book p1019)

questions.sec: Hemochromatosis organ pathology, genetic IOC and phlebotomy
questions.q: A 52-year-old man presents with chronic pain in his 2nd and 3rd MCP joints, loss of libido, and dark slate-grey skin bronzing. Transferrin saturation is 72% and serum ferritin is 2400 ng/mL. HFE testing confirms homozygous C282Y mutation. Which of his clinical manifestations is irreversible despite phlebotomy?
opts: MCP joint arthropathy and testicular hypogonadism
questions.exp: Joint arthritis and gonadal damage are irreversible manifestations of hereditary hemochromatosis. (Book p1019)

units.title: Wilson's disease inheritance, Menkes comparison and copper transport
units.guide: Autosomal recessive ATP7B on chromosome 13q, Menkes ATP7A on X chromosome (3 months, seizures, brittle hair), daily intake 2-5 mg with 1 mg absorption via DMT1, metallothionein 3-year capacity, fundamental defect in ceruloplasmin incorporation and biliary excretion, apoceruloplasmin false elevation, and acute adolescent clues (low Hb, low cholinesterase, mild transaminitis, low ALP).

units.title: Wilson's presentations, jaundice types, tennis-racquet cristae and Neuro-Wilson's
units.guide: Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with low ALP (copper-zinc competition), chronic asymptomatic transaminitis (<150 U/L), mixed cirrhosis on ultrasound, maximum jaundice tendency across pre-hepatic, hepatic, and post-hepatic forms, tennis-racquet mitochondrial cristae on EM, glycogenated nuclei, zone 1 periportal predilection, and 10-year latency to Neuro-Wilson's.

units.title: Neurological features, Kayser-Fleischer ring, sunflower cataract and systemic pathology
units.guide: Dysarthria (m/c), Parkinsonism, Risus sardonicus, wing-beating tremors, Kayser-Fleischer rings in Descemet's membrane (60-65% hepatic, 95-99% neuro, seen in PBC/PSC, regresses with chelation), sunflower cataract, hypoparathyroidism, proximal RTA Type 2, and recurrent spontaneous abortion.

units.title: Diagnostic ceruloplasmin algorithm, biopsy cut-off, Nazar index and chelation
units.guide: Ceruloplasmin cut-offs (>20 rule out, 10-20 intermediate with free copper spill, <10 confirmatory), liver biopsy >250 µg/g dry weight by neutron activation/atomic absorption, false elevation causes, Nazar prognostic index (bilirubin, AST, PT), D-penicillamine (250 mg to 1.5 g empty stomach, lupus/myasthenia/pyridoxine 25 mg risks), trientine, tetrathiomolybdate, and zinc (50 mg TDS).

units.title: Brain MRI signs in Wilson's and Hereditary Hemochromatosis genetics
units.guide: Face of giant panda, basal ganglia and thalamic hyperintensity, bisected and Mercedes-Benz trisected pontine signs, Bright Claustrum sign, Hereditary Hemochromatosis autosomal recessive HFE gene on 6p (4th-5th decade), homozygous C282Y vs heterozygous PCT/NASH, juvenile non-HFE genes (HJV, TfR2, hepcidin), and alcohol acceleration.

units.title: Iron transport pathophysiology, screening saturation and liver MRI
units.guide: Apical DMT-1 entry, basolateral ferroportin export, hepatic hepcidin negative regulation, HFE mutation failure, transferrin saturation > 45% as best screening test (S.Fe/TIBC x 100), low TIBC, Prussian blue periportal hemosiderosis, and liver MRI low intensity with splenic sparing.

units.title: Systemic manifestations, genetic IOC, phlebotomy and irreversible damage
units.guide: Type 3c bronze DM, DCM > RCMP, CPPD arthropathy with hook-like osteophytes in 2nd/3rd MCP and wrists, pituitary stalk hypogonadotropic hypogonadism triad, slate-grey bronzing, HFE C282Y mutation IOC, weekly phlebotomy (target ferritin <50-500 ng/mL), subcutaneous desferrioxamine, irreversible joint and gonadal damage, and persistent post-transplant HCC risk.
